about: The postcommunio of the formulary “Third Sunday after Epiphany” in the 1962 Roman Missal.

s01.translation: O Lord, You graciously allow us to partake of such great mysteries; we beseech You to deign truly to fit us for their effects. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, Your Son, who lives and reigns with You in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever.

alignments.gloss: We, whom You graciously allow, O Lord, to partake of such great mysteries,
may deign truly to fit us for their effects

w001.explanation: “We” makes explicit the praying subject already carried by quaesumus. Quos refers to the people whom the Lord grants the use of the mysteries: it is the accusative subject of uti, not a nominative relative describing the Lord.

w004.explanation: The use of the mysteries is a gift from the Lord, not merely permission to use them. Largiris conveys generous giving, while uti has an active sense here.

w009.explanation: The petition asks God to fit us for the effects of the mysteries, to which eorum refers. Effectibus can be dative or ablative in form, and aptare also admits an ablative naming what someone is furnished with. Its written form alone does not decide between fitting us for their effects and furnishing us with them.
